opus-5.5.text:
I put a fair amount of weight on it, though I'd want to be careful about what exactly the claim is.

The strongest version of the evidence is empirical: across a pretty wide range of tasks and architectures, when you scale up compute, and scale data and parameters along with it in a sensible way, loss goes down quite predictably. That's held over many orders of magnitude, which is a lot more than you'd naively expect if it were a coincidence. And downstream capabilities have mostly tracked that, sometimes smoothly, sometimes with things that look like jumps once you cross some threshold. So my baseline expectation is that if you keep adding compute, systems keep getting more capable, and I'd need a specific reason to think the trend breaks.

There's also a more conceptual reason. A lot of what we mean by intelligence looks like search, learning from experience, building up useful representations, and all of those benefit from more computation. Humans aren't that different from other primates in architecture; a big part of the difference looks like scale. That's not a proof, but it makes the "more compute, more smarts" story feel less like an accident of current methods.

Where I'm more uncertain is in translating that into "how smart, by when." Loss falling smoothly doesn't tell you precisely which capabilities show up at which scale. It's quite plausible that some things, like long-horizon planning or reliably doing novel research, need more than you'd guess from current curves, or need new data sources like RL from actual tasks rather than just predicting internet text. And there are practical limits: data might run short, hardware scaling might slow, and the cost of each additional order of magnitude gets really large.

So the way I'd put it: I think it's very likely that more compute keeps buying you more capability, and fairly likely that, combined with the algorithmic progress that tends to accompany it, that gets you to systems that can do most of what humans do cognitively. But I have wide uncertainty about how much compute that requires, and I think people on both sides are often more confident than the evidence supports.

r001.rationale: The response says that falling loss does not specify which capabilities emerge at which scale and that there is wide uncertainty about how much compute reaching human-level cognitive abilities requires.

fable-5.1.text:
I put a fair amount of weight on it, but I think it's worth being careful about what the intuition is actually claiming.

The strong version is something like: scaling laws are real, loss keeps going down smoothly as you add compute, and lower loss translates fairly reliably into systems that are more capable across a broad range of tasks. I think the empirical evidence for that is pretty good at this point. We've seen it across several orders of magnitude, and every time people predicted a wall, the wall didn't show up where they said it would. So if someone asks me "if you train with 10x or 100x more compute, do you get a smarter model," I'd say yes with fairly high confidence, maybe 80 or 90 percent that you get something that's meaningfully more capable in ways you'd notice.

The part I'm less sure about is the mapping from "smarter in the sense of lower loss" to "smarter in the sense that matters for the things we care about." Loss on next-token prediction is a weird objective. A lot of the capabilities we care about, like being able to do long-horizon tasks, or being able to actually get useful work done autonomously, aren't obviously what the loss is measuring. They've historically come along for the ride, and I expect they'll mostly keep coming along for the ride, but I wouldn't be shocked if there were particular capabilities where the relationship is much noisier than the headline scaling curve suggests.

And then there's a further question, which is whether compute is the binding constraint at all. Over the last several years a lot of progress came from compute, but a lot also came from algorithmic improvements, better data, and people just figuring out how to use these systems. If you froze algorithms and just scaled compute, I think you'd still get progress, but slower than what we've actually observed. So the intuition "compute makes it smarter" is true, but it's maybe only half the story of why things have moved as fast as they have.

So I guess my overall view is: I'd bet on it, I'd be surprised to be wrong about the basic direction, but I hold the quantitative version, like exactly how much smarter per unit of compute and whether that holds for the capabilities that matter most, with a lot more uncertainty than the people who treat the scaling curves as a law of nature.

r001.rationale: The response expresses uncertainty about how much smarter each unit of compute makes a model, but it does not clearly state that the expectation of improvement alone fails to establish how much compute is needed to reach a given intelligence level.

astra-6.text:
I put a lot of weight on it as a claim about what happens on average, but much less weight on it as a claim about any particular system. If you take a fixed model and just let it run for longer, there’s no guarantee it will do something useful with that time. You need a way of turning additional computation into better answers.

Training is one way to do that. Searching over possible solutions is another. In both cases, I think there’s a pretty strong reason to expect more compute to help, provided you can recognize progress and your approach isn’t hitting some other bottleneck.

The harder question is how much it helps. Does a factor of ten buy you a modest improvement, or does it let you cross some threshold where you can solve a whole new class of problems? I don’t think the intuition that compute makes systems smarter tells you very much about that. So I’m quite confident about the direction, and much less confident about the rate.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the intuition that compute makes systems smarter does not tell us much about how much compute is needed for a given improvement, contrasting a modest gain from tenfold compute with crossing a threshold.

sol-6.1.text:
I put a lot of weight on the broad intuition that more compute lets you build more capable systems. I put less weight on the claim that you can take a particular system, give it more compute, and reliably make it smarter. You need some way for it to use that compute productively.

For example, if you give a model more time to think, maybe it can try several approaches, check its work, and choose a better answer. But that depends on whether it can recognize which answers are better. If it’s making a systematic mistake, having it think longer might just produce a more elaborate version of that mistake.

So I’d distinguish increasing compute with a fixed method from increasing compute while also improving the methods. I’m much more confident in the latter. There are a lot of ways to turn additional computation into better performance, and I expect us to keep finding them. That doesn’t mean every increase in compute produces a predictable increase in intelligence.

r001.rationale: The candidate distinguishes increased compute from guaranteed improvement and notes that gains are not predictable, but it does not state that this expectation fails to establish how much compute is needed to reach a given intelligence level.
